items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we'll see how the concept of a relation can be extended to subsets of Cartesian products containing more than three factors.

Content:
First, recall that a binary relation over [MATH: A] is any subset of the Cartesian product [MATH: A\times A = A^2.] We can extend this idea as follows:

Content:
> A ternary ([MATH: 3]-ary) relation [MATH: R] over the set [MATH: A] is a subset of the Cartesian product [MATH: A \times A \times A = A^3]
> [MATH: R \subseteq A^3]

Content:
For example, consider the relation [MATH: R] defined on [MATH: A = \big\{1, 2, \ldots, 10 \big\}] by
[MATH: (x,y,z) \in R
\qquad \Leftrightarrow \qquad
x + y \equiv z \quad (\textrm{mod} \: 4).]

Content:
Note that, for example,

Content:
- [MATH: (2,3,9) \in R] since [MATH: 2 + 3 \equiv 9 \: (\textrm{mod} \: 4),] but
- [MATH: (1,1,1) \not\in R] since [MATH: 1+1 \not\equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod} \: 4).]

Content:
Similar to binary relations, there is no need for the factors of the Cartesian product always to be the same set:

Content:
> A ternary ([MATH: 3]-ary) relation [MATH: R] over the sets [MATH: A,B,C] is a subset of [MATH: A \times B \times C{:}]
> [MATH: R \subseteq A \times B \times C]

Content:
Let's see some more examples.

items.title: Identifying True Statements Given a Finite Ternary Relation

sections.normalized_html:

  1. [MATH: (2,2,4)\in R]

  2. [MATH: (3,1,3)\in R]

  3. [MATH: (1,3,4)\in R]

1. [MATH: (2,2,4)\in R]
2. [MATH: (3,1,3)\in R]

sections.normalized_html:
A ternary ([MATH: 3]-ary) relation [MATH: R] over the sets [MATH: A,B,C] is a subset of the Cartesian product [MATH: A imes B imes C.] [MATH: R \subseteq A imes B imes C]

In this case, we have [MATH: (x,y,z) \in R \subseteq A^3] if and only if [MATH: xyz = 9.]

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn:

  • Statement I is false. We have [MATH: (2,2,4) otin R] since [MATH: 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 = 16 eq 9.]

  • Statement II is true. We have [MATH: (3,1,3) \in R] since [MATH: 3 \cdot 1 \cdot 3 = 9.]

  • Statement III is false. We have [MATH: (1,3,4) otin R] since [MATH: 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 12 eq 9.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

Item 6 — Example: Identifying True Statements Given a Infinite N-ary Relation

Example Prompt:
Given the relation [MATH: R] on [MATH: \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})^4] defined by
[MATH: (A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4) \in R
\qquad \Leftrightarrow \qquad
A_1 \cup A_2 = A_3 \cup A_4,]
which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \big( \{1\}, \{3\}, \emptyset, \{1,3\}\big) \in R]
2. [MATH: \big( \mathbb{N}, \emptyset, \{2\}, \{2,3\}\big) \in R]
3. [MATH: \big( \{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{4\}\big) \in R]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A [MATH: n]-ary relation [MATH: R] over the sets [MATH: A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n] is a subset of the Cartesian product [MATH: A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_n.]

[MATH: R \subseteq A_1 \times A_2 \times \cdots \times A_n]

In this case, we have [MATH: (A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4) \in R \subseteq \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})^4] if and only if [MATH: A_1 \cup A_2 = A_3 \cup A_4.]

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn:

- Statement I is true. We have [MATH: \big( \{1\}, \{3\}, \emptyset, \{1,3\}\big) \in R] since
[MATH: \{1\} \cup \{3\} = \{1,3\}= \emptyset \cup \{1,3\}.]
- Statement II is false. We have [MATH: \big( \mathbb{N}, \emptyset, \{2\}, \{2,3\}\big) \not\in R] since
[MATH: \mathbb{N} \cup \emptyset = \mathbb{N} \neq \{2,3\} = \{2\} \cup \{2,3\}.]
- Statement III is false. We have [MATH: \big( \{1\}, \{2\}, \{3\}, \{4\}\big) \not\in R] since
[MATH: \{1\} \cup \{2\} = \{1,2\} \neq \{3,4\} = \{3\} \cup \{4\}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
